newsitem.title: CHINA: China sees employee buyouts to save small firms.
newsitem.headline: China sees employee buyouts to save small firms.

text.p: China unveiled on Thursday new measures to reform small state enterprises, encouraging employee buyouts of struggling firms the government no longer wants and promoting the long-taboo concept of private ownership.

A front-page commentary in the China Securities newspaper contained the boldest public call yet for an official go-ahead for private ownership -- a reference to the transfer of state assets into non-state hands.

It called for "re-establishing private ownership on the basis of socialisation of productivity" in a commentary as part of a stream of government propaganda to set the scene for a crucial Communist Party congress in September or October that will set policy guidelines for the next five years.

While China's communist leaders have allowed private enterprise since the mid-1980s, they have yet to provide a level playing field and have strongly opposed diversification in ownership of state firms -- the core of their socialist system.
Officials on Thursday promoted a new means of ownership to help the party to hive off the smaller of China's estimated 350,000 lumbering state firms.

Cooperative shareholding ownership, already widespread among low-technology rural enterprises, should be pursued among small urban state-owned firms that are running out of steam in China's new sink-or-swim marketplace, state media and officials said.

"The merit is that this can promote initiative of employees and enterprise efficiency with employees responsible for their own firms," said an official of the State Commission for Restructuring Economic Systems.
Employees could own shares in enterprises, pooling their funds to run the firms jointly, but could not trade their shares, he said.
"Exercise of the cooperative shareholding system makes use of management responsibility of enterprise assets," the People's Daily said, giving details of the new system.
"(This) raises the level of concern and sense of risk of workers toward an enterprise, increases the cohesive forces, awakens the motivation of workers," it said.
"(This) separates the government from the enterprise and speeds up transformation of the enterprise into a competitive market force responsible for its own management...its own development," it said.

The system, effectively employee buyouts of China's tens of thousands of smaller urban state firms, entitled stockholders to one vote per person regardless of how many stocks they held but with a dividend according to shares held, officials said.

Such employee buyouts had proved an effective way to reduce the high levels of outstanding debt to banks, since banks would reallocate the credit at low rates of interest to the new owners of the enterprise, another official of the State Commission for Restructuring Economic Systems said.

Officials acknowledged that the new methods were effectively little different from promoting private ownership as a means of reviving China's state firms, but stopped short of using a term that has been taboo for decades.

China's leaders have agreed that tackling quickly the restructuring of the huge -- and flagging -- state sector is among the most crucial reforms remaining to be implemented under late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping's vision of a "socialist market economy".

However, they are locked in debate over how to proceed with the ideologically fraught issue of nurturing the private sector and seen allowing state firms to flow away from government ownership and into private hands.

"This is one of the main methods the government could use to provide employment to people made jobless by restructuring of state-owned firms," said one Chinese economist. "There are plenty of jobs that can be created in the non-state sector."
